## **Meaning in Language**
<br>
.pull-left[
- so far this semester, we've focused on the form or structure of language<br><br>
- **Morphology**: study of the <u>structure</u> of words
  - morphemes, morphological processes, morphological trees<br><br>
- **Syntax**: study of the <u>structure</u> of sentences
  - parts of speech, constituents, phrase structure rules, syntax trees
]

.pull-left[
## **Meaning in Language**
<br>
of course, language is **NOT** just structure – language has **meaning** – and we've mentioned meaning on several occasions:<br><br>
- **Morphology**
  - morphemes are the smallest linguistic unit with <u><i>meaning</i></u>
  - derivation changes a word's core <u><i>meaning</i></u>
  - order of affixation reflects a word's <u><i>meaning</i></u><br><br>
- **Syntax**
  - parts of speech can be defined based on their <u><i>meaning</i></u>
  - ambiguous sentences like '<i>The girl saw the bear with the telescope</i>' show us that syntactic structures contribute to the <u><i>meaning</i></u> of sentences
]
.pull-right[
<br>

<br><br>
<img src="../pic/1019/telen.png" width="70%">
</div>
]

## **Meaning in Language**
<br>
in this and the next unit, we're going to focus on **meaning** more specifically and we can differentiate three **types** of linguistic meaning:<br><br>

**literal meaning**<br>
  - **Semantics** studies <u>*literal meaning*</u> in language <br><br>
  
<span style="color:green"><b>implied meaning</b></span><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>Pragmatics</b></span> studies <u>*implied meaning*</u> in language <br><br>
  
<span style="color:blue"><b>social meaning</b></span><br>
  - <span style="color:blue"><b>Sociolinguistics</b></span> and <span style="color:blue"><b>Linguistic Anthropology</b></span> study <u>*social meaning*</u>

  
---
## **Literal Meaning and Implied Meaning**
<br>
.pull-left[
- as a system for communicating ideas, language must have **meaning**<br><br>
- but meaning in language goes **beyond** the **literal**<br><br>
  - imagine the following conversation:<br><br>
  **A**: <i>Do you want to go out tonight</i>?<br>
  **B**: <i>I have an exam in the morning</i><br><br>
  - what has B literally said?<br><br>
  - what has B implied that they have not said explicitly?<br><br>
- as in this example, much of what we say has different levels of **literal** and **implied** meaning
]
.pull-right[
<br>
<img src="../pic/1019/long.jpg" width="100%">
]

---
## **Social Meaning**
<br>
- language also has **social meaning**, since it's a tool for **social interaction**:<br><br>
  - we use **small talk** to establish and reinforce social bonds with others
  - the way we speak can indicate our attitude toward others (friendliness, solidarity, irritation…)<br><br>
- we actively **choose** to speak a particular way to convey a particular social identity<br><br>
  - good morning</i> to a professor<br>
  - 'sup</i> to a friend<br>
  - do we usually do it other way around?<br><br>
  - homosexual voice? [just an example, not sterotype]<br><br>
- we often unconsciously **accommodate to the speech** of people we like, adopting phrases and speech patterns from them without even noticing it<br><br>
  - have you noticed your speech changing since you came to college?
---
## **Social Meaning**
<br>
.pull-left[
language **varies** by region, community, and other social factors<br><br>
- so the way we speak often **conveys information** like where we're from, our age, gender, etc.<br><br>
- we often strongly **identify** with the language and dialect we grew up speaking<br><br>
- we can actively use language to **signal our membership** in certain communities<br><br>
  - A: <i>Did you eat my cake</i>?<br>
    B: <i>I <b>never</b> ate your cake</i>.
]
.pull-right[
<br>
<img src="../pic/1019/british.jpg" width="100%">
]

.pull-left[
## **Semantics**
<br>
<img src="../pic/1019/coffeeortea.jpg" width="85%">
]
.pull-right[
<br>
- in this unit, we'll focus on **Semantics** – the literal meaning of language<br><br>
- we can identify two levels of semantics: **lexical semantics** and **compositional semantics**<br><br>
- **lexical semantics** – the meaning of words
  - lexicon refers to a speaker's mental vocabulary; words are known as lexical items, but lexical items can also include common multi-word expressions<br><br>
- **compositional semantics** – the meaning of sentences
  - we said <u><i>A girl saw a bear with a telescope.</i></u> has two different meanings, and these meanings depend on syntax
  - meaning of a sentence = meaning of words + meaning of structure
]

---
## **Lexical Meaning**
<br>
**lexical semantics** studies the **meaning of words** and lexical meaning is **conventional** and **arbitrary**<br><br>
- lexical meaning is **conventional**<br><br>
1. words mean what they mean because we agree as a speech community that's what they mean – that is, words are defined by **social convention**<br><br>
2. consider words with slang meanings like <i><u>sick</u></i> 'amazing, excellent'<br><br>
  - how did <i><u>sick</u></i> come to mean 'great'? <br><br>
  - someone starting using it with that meaning, and it caught on – the rest of the community agreed it can be used that way, too<br><br>
3. same thing with **technological terms** like <i><u>mouse</u></i>, <i><u>screen</u></i>, <i><u>tablet</u></i>, even <i><u>computer</u></i>:<br><br>
  - all of these words originally had other meanings, but when we invented new technology and needed a name for it, we agreed these words can have new meanings<br><br>

---
## **Lexical Meaning**
<br>
**lexical semantics** studies the **meaning of words** and lexical meaning is **conventional** and **arbitrary**<br><br>
- lexical meaning is **arbitrary**
  - there is no inherent connection between the sound of a word and its meaning<br><br>
- we know this because:
  - same **sounds** can have different **meanings** in different languages:<br>
  <span style="color:green"><b>Spanish</b></span> <i>taco</i> 'taco' vs. <span style="color:green"><b>Japanese</b></span> <i>tako</i> 'octopus'<br>
  <span style="color:green"><b>English</b></span> <i>eat</i> 'eat' vs. <span style="color:green"><b>Kazakh</b></span> <i>it</i> 'dog'<br><br>
  - same **meaning** can be conveyed with different **sounds** in different languages:<br>
  <span style="color:green"><b>English</b></span> <i>dog</i> vs. <span style="color:green"><b>Spanish</b></span> <i>perro</i><br><br>
  - meaning and sound of words can **change over time**:<br>
  <i>nice</i> 'foolish' > 'kind', <i>knight</i> [knixt] > [najt]<br><br>
- main exception: **onomatopoeia** – words that mimic sounds
  - even **onomatopoeia** can be a bit arbitrary: cockadoodledoo, quiquiriquí, kokekokko, wowo
  
---

there are two ways of thinking about a word's meaning:<br><br>
**sense** and **reference**<br><br>
- the **sense** of a word is:
  - the mental concept of a word's meaning
  - a description of this mental concept: dictionary definition<br><br>
- for instance, the sense of fruit might be:
  - a seed-bearing structure in flowering plants
]

there are two ways of thinking about a word's meaning:<br><br>
**sense** and **reference**<br><br>
- the **reference** of a word is:
  - the set of things in the world that the word refers to
  - each thing the word refers to is a **referent** of the word<br><br>
- the reference of the word fruit would include:
  - the apple I had for breakfast
  - the bananas they have at Cafe West
  - the oranges they sell at Costco...
]

- defining words by **reference** helps us understand how we can
categorise new items we come across:
  - by comparing them to the referents we already know<br><br>
- it's also more in line with how we **learn** words:
  - we don't learn what an animal is by learning that it's a
"<u><i>multicellular eukaryotic organism [in] Animalia</i></u>" (Wikipedia)<br><br>
  - we learn what an animal is by learning that a **puppy** is an animal and a **kitty** is an animal and a **froggy** is an animal...<br><br>
  - we learn what a fruit is by observing what our caregivers call fruit
]

in this class, we'll define words by **reference**, which is the **set** of things in the world (referents) that the word refers to<br><br>
- once we define a word as a **set** or collection of things, we can also **compare** the sets of things that different words refer to<br><br>

1. some words refer to **entirely different** sets of things
2. sometimes there is overlap between **two sets** of referents<br><br>

is there any reference overlap in each pair below?
  - <span style="color:green">dog</span> vs. <span style="color:blue">animal</span>
  - <span style="color:green">dog</span> vs. <span style="color:orange">canine</span>
  - <span style="color:green">dog</span> vs. <span style="color:deeppink">husky</span>

]

## **Semantic Relations**
<br>
- **synonym:** words that have the same reference / refer to the same set of things in the world<br><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>drinks</b></span> and <span style="color:green"><b>beverages</b></span><br><br>
- **hypernym:** words whose reference is a **superset** of another words reference<br><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>student</b></span> is a hypernym to <span style="color:green"><b>linguistics student</b></span><br><br>
- **hyponym:** words whose reference is a **subset** of another words reference<br><br>
  - <span style="color:green"><b>dog</b></span> is a hyponym to <span style="color:green"><b>mammal</b></span><br><br>
- **antonym:** words that have opposite meanings
]

## **Semantic Relations: Antonyms**
<br>
.pull-left[
**antonym:** words that have opposite meanings, and it turns out to be difficult to define in terms of reference<br><br>
- **complementary pairs:** items that can't be in both categories
  - <span style="color:green"><b>alive</b></span> vs. <span style="color:green"><b>dead</b></span><br><br>
  
- **gradable pairs:** opposite ends of a scale
  - <span style="color:green"><b>young</b></span> vs. <span style="color:green"><b>old</b></span><br><br>
  
- **reverses:** opposite directions
  - <span style="color:green"><b>up</b></span> vs. <span style="color:green"><b>down</b></span><br><br>
  
- **converses:** same action, different perspective
  - <span style="color:green"><b>buy</b></span> vs. <span style="color:green"><b>sell</b></span><br><br>
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/1019/seman4.jpg" width="100%">
]

## **Compositional Semantics**
<br>
- so we've seen some ideas about **lexical semantics** – the meaning of words (or lexical items)<br><br>
- beyond words, phrases and sentence can also have meaning - **compositional semantics**<br><br>
- **COMPOSITIONALITY in semantics**:<br><br>
  - the meaning of a **complex** expression is due to
  1. the meaning of its parts (i.e., lexical meaning);
  2. how these parts are **combined** (i.e., syntactic structure)<br><br>
- compare these two sentences:
  (a) <i>It is <span style="color:green">snowing</span> outside</i>.
  (b) <i>It is <span style="color:green">sunny</span> outside</i>.<br><br>
- both sentences are formed by <i><u>it is ... outside</u></i> + a <span style="color:green"><i>weather word</i></span>
- yet they cannot be true at the same time, and which one is true depends on <span style="color:green"><i>snowing</i></span> and <span style="color:green"><i>sunny</i></span>

## **Truth Values**
<br><br>
.pull-left[
- part of a sentence's meaning is its **truth value**: is it <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span> or <span style="color:green; font-variant: small-caps"><b>false</b></span><br><br>
- What is the **truth value** of the following sentences?<br><br>
  1. Earth is a planet.<br><br>
  2. Fish are birds.<br><br>
  3. Mars is in the Solar System.<br><br>
  4. Cats are animals.
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/1019/truthvalue.jpg" width="90%">
]

---
## **Complex Truth Values**
<br>

- some sentences make multiple propositions, each of which has its own truth value:
<span style="color:white">- the truth value of a sentence <span style="color:white"><b>depends on</b></span> the truth value of its propositions</span>
<span style="color:white">- all of the propositions in a sentence must be <span style="color:white; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span> for the entire sentence to be <span style="color:white; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span></span><br><br>

.pull-left[
- <span style="color:blue"><i>Earth is a rocky planet</i>.</span><br><br>
  - <u>proposition 1</u>: Earth is a planet. <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span></span>
  - <u>proposition 2</u>: Earth is rocky. <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span></span><br><br>
  <span style="color:white">- sentence truth value: <span style="color:white; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span></span><br><br>
- <span style="color:deeppink"><i>Merlin speaks Kazakh and Greek</i>.</span><br><br>
  - <u>proposition 1</u>: Merlin speaks Kazakh. <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span>
  - <u>proposition 2</u>: Merlin speaks Greek. <span style="color:green; font-variant: small-caps"><b>false</b></span><br><br>
  <span style="color:white">- sentence truth value: <span style="color:white; font-variant: small-caps"><b>false</b></span></span>
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/1019/seman3.png" width="90%">
]

---
## **Complex Truth Values**
<br>
- some sentences make multiple propositions, each of which has its own truth value:
- the truth value of a sentence **depends on** the truth value of its propositions
- all of the propositions in a sentence must be <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span> for the entire sentence to be <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span><br><br>

.pull-left[
- <span style="color:blue"><i>Earth is a rocky planet</i>.</span><br><br>
  - <u>proposition 1</u>: Earth is a planet. <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span>
  - <u>proposition 2</u>: Earth is rocky. <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span><br><br>
  - sentence truth value: <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span><br><br>
- <span style="color:deeppink"><i>Merlin speaks Kazakh and Greek</i>.</span><br><br>
  - <u>proposition 1</u>: Merlin speaks Kazakh. <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span>
  - <u>proposition 2</u>: Merlin speaks Greek. <span style="color:green; font-variant: small-caps"><b>false</b></span><br><br>
  - sentence truth value: <span style="color:green; font-variant: small-caps"><b>false</b></span>
]
.pull-right[
<img src="../pic/1019/seman3.png" width="90%">
]

---
## **Complex Truth Values**
<br>
.pull-left[
<img src="../pic/1019/seman2.jpg" width="65%">
]
.pull-right[
- a sentence might also give rise to other, **unspoken propositions** –
  often related through synonyms, hypernyms, and hyponyms<br><br>
- the sentence <i><u>I have a dog.</u><i> gives rise to other propositions:<br><br>
  - I have a pet.<br><br>
  - My pet is a canine.<br><br>
  - My pet is an animal.<br><br>
- all of these propositions must also be <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span> for the sentence to be <span style="color:#CC0033; font-variant: small-caps"><b>true</b></span>:<br><br>
  - If <u><i>my pet is an animal</i></u> is false, then <u><i>I have a dog</i></u> cannot be true.
]
.pull-right[

]
